context.concept_name: matplotlib figure and axes object model

coverage.learning_objective: Recognize matplotlib's Figure/Axes object model: identify which calls create the Figure vs. the Axes, and create a Figure with one Axes to plot on.

required_facts.statement: Matplotlib graphs data on Figures, and each Figure can contain one or more Axes, which is the area where data is actually plotted.
fig, ax = plt.subplots() creates a Figure and one Axes together, giving explicit variables for both objects.
Plotting calls such as ax.plot(x, y) draw onto that specific Axes object.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you have this week's delivery times -- 18, 22, 26, 19, 30 minutes -- and you want to see them as a graph instead of a list of numbers. Matplotlib is the library that draws that graph, but it draws onto two different kinds of object, not just "a plot". Matplotlib graphs data on Figures, and each Figure can contain one or more Axes, which is the area where data is actually plotted.

The Figure is the overall canvas: the whole window or image you eventually display or save. An Axes is one plotting area that lives inside that Figure -- the rectangle with its own x- and y-axis where lines, bars, or points are actually drawn. A single Figure can hold more than one Axes, but even the simplest plot needs at least one.

After `import matplotlib.pyplot as plt`, `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` creates a Figure and one Axes together, giving explicit variables for both objects: `fig` refers to the whole canvas, and `ax` refers to the one plotting area inside it.

Plotting calls such as `ax.plot(x, y)` draw onto that specific Axes object. `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` followed by `ax.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` draws the week's delivery times as a line onto `ax`. `fig` itself doesn't receive any plotted data directly -- it just holds the Axes that does.

With `plt.subplots()`, you get a Figure and an Axes first, then call a plotting method on the Axes, not the Figure. Keeping the two straight -- Figure is the canvas, Axes is where the data goes -- makes plotting calls like `ax.plot()` easier to read.

video_need.reason: The Figure-as-canvas / Axes-as-plotting-area relationship is a spatial container relationship that is easier to picture when it is highlighted on screen and watched being created and drawn onto, though the text's canvas framing and the worked fig/ax example already make the idea workable from text alone.

required_facts.statement: plt.subplots(figsize=(width, height)) sets the figure's dimensions; figsize is a (width, height) tuple which is interpreted as (width, height, 'in'), and its default is rcParams['figure.figsize'], which defaults to [6.4, 4.8].
tight_layout() automatically adjusts subplot parameters so that the subplot(s) fit into the figure area; it works by checking the extents of tick labels, axis labels, and titles.
tight_layout() can be called as plt.tight_layout() or fig.tight_layout().

teaching_blocks.content: `plt.subplots(figsize=(width, height))` sets the figure's dimensions. `figsize` is a (width, height) tuple, measured in inches, and its default is `rcParams['figure.figsize']`, which itself defaults to `[6.4, 4.8]`. `fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))` makes a wider-than-default figure, 8 inches by 4 inches, and `fig.tight_layout()` then adjusts the spacing to fit.

`tight_layout()` automatically adjusts subplot parameters so the subplot(s) fit into the figure area; it works by checking the extents of tick labels, axis labels, and titles. It can be called as `plt.tight_layout()` or `fig.tight_layout()`.

context.concept_name: Basic plot creation with the pyplot interface

coverage.learning_objective: Create a basic plot from data using matplotlib's pyplot interface, with the correct plt.plot() argument form.

required_facts.statement: plt.plot(y) called with a single array argument treats it as the y-values and automatically generates the x-values starting from 0.
plt.plot(x, y) called with two array arguments plots the y-values against the given x-values.

teaching_blocks.content: You have already seen `ax.plot(x, y)` draw onto an Axes you created with `plt.subplots()`. pyplot also has its own `plot()` function, called directly as `plt.plot()`, and it accepts data in two different forms.

`plt.plot(y)` called with a single array argument treats it as the y-values and automatically generates the x-values starting from 0. Given just the delivery times `[18, 22, 26, 19, 30]`, `plt.plot([18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` plots those five values against the automatic x-positions 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

`plt.plot(x, y)` called with two array arguments plots the y-values against the given x-values instead. `plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` plots the same five delivery times, but now against the day numbers 1 through 5 you supplied, rather than the automatic 0-based positions.
Both forms call the same function and produce a similar-looking line; the only difference is whether you hand `plot()` an explicit x-axis or let it fill one in for you starting at 0.

video_need.reason: Seeing the one-array call auto-number its x-axis from 0, side by side with the two-array call using the supplied x-values, makes the difference between the two forms concrete in a way the text's description approximates.

coverage.learning_objective: Create a bar chart with matplotlib to compare a numeric value across discrete categories, aligning bars to a common baseline.

required_facts.statement: plt.bar(x, height) (or ax.bar(x, height)) makes a bar plot with bars positioned at the given x coordinates and given heights, with the baseline defaulting to 0.
A bar chart is a common chart type for graphing categorical data or data sorted into groups.
Bar charts are easy to interpret because the eye is good at comparing lengths when the objects being compared are aligned to a common baseline.
Categorical variables such as names can be passed directly as the x argument to plt.bar() (for example plt.bar(names, values)), rather than only numeric x-positions.

misconceptions.statement: A bar's baseline can start at any value without distorting the comparison.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you want to compare average delivery time across three cities -- Lagos, Abuja, and Kano -- rather than look at individual deliveries. A bar chart is a common chart type for graphing categorical data or data sorted into groups, which fits this comparison exactly.

`plt.bar(x, height)` (or `ax.bar(x, height)`) makes a bar plot with bars positioned at the given x coordinates and given heights, with the baseline defaulting to 0. Categorical variables such as names can be passed directly as the x argument, rather than only numeric x-positions: `city_avg = orders.groupby("city")["delivery_time_minutes"].mean()` stores one average per city, with the city names as its index, and `plt.bar(city_avg.index, city_avg)` plots those three city names directly as the bars' x-positions, with each city's average as its bar height.

Bar charts are easy to interpret because the eye is good at comparing lengths when the objects being compared are aligned to a common baseline -- here, every bar starts at 0, so the bar for Kano simply looks taller than Lagos's because its average delivery time is higher.

It can seem harmless to start the bars at some value other than 0 -- say at 20 minutes, to make small differences between cities stand out. That distorts the comparison. A bar chart is easy to read because the eye compares bar lengths from a common baseline, so the lengths themselves have to stay true to the values. If Kano averages 30 minutes and Lagos 25, bars that start at 20 are 10 and 5 units tall: Kano's bar looks twice as long as Lagos's even though its average is only 5 minutes higher. Keep the baseline at 0.

video_need.reason: Why the shared zero baseline matters is a before/after comparison -- the same three city averages rendered with a shared baseline versus a shifted one look like they tell different stories, which is far more convincing seen than described.

coverage.learning_objective: Create a histogram with matplotlib to visualize a numeric variable's distribution, and adjust the bins parameter to change how the data is binned.

required_facts.statement: plt.hist(x, bins=...) uses numpy.histogram to bin the data in x, count the number of values in each bin, and draw the result as bars.

The bins parameter defaults to rcParams['hist.bins'], which defaults to 10; passing an integer sets that many equal-width bins, passing a sequence sets explicit bin edges, and passing a string such as 'auto' selects a binning strategy.

teaching_blocks.content: A bar chart compares categories, but delivery times themselves are a numeric variable, and you might instead want to see how those times are distributed -- how many deliveries were fast, how many were slow.

`plt.hist(x, bins=...)` uses `numpy.histogram` to bin the data in `x`, count the number of values in each bin, and draw the result as bars. `plt.hist(orders["delivery_time_minutes"])` bins every delivery's time and shows how many deliveries fall in each time range.

The `bins` parameter defaults to `rcParams['hist.bins']`, which defaults to 10; passing an integer sets that many equal-width bins, passing a sequence sets explicit bin edges, and passing a string such as `'auto'` selects a binning strategy. `plt.hist(orders["delivery_time_minutes"], bins=5)` groups the data into 5 equal-width bins instead of the default 10. Each bar's height shows how many deliveries fall into that bin, so a taller bar means more deliveries took that range of time.

coverage.learning_objective: Create a box plot with matplotlib to visualize a numeric variable's quartiles, median, and outliers, optionally comparing several groups.

required_facts.statement: plt.boxplot(x) (or ax.boxplot(x)) draws a box plot from the data in x; it accepts array-like data and can draw one or more boxes.

The box extends from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3) of the data, with a line at the median. The whiskers extend from the box to the farthest data point lying within 1.5x the interquartile range (IQR) from the box; points past the end of the whiskers are flier points (outliers).
Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side.
Passing a sequence of 1D arrays as x draws one box for each array in the sequence; tick_labels=[...] labels each boxplot's tick accordingly instead of leaving it as a numeric value.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you want to compare the full spread of delivery times across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano -- not just their averages, but how spread out and how extreme each city's times get. Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side.

`plt.boxplot(x)` (or `ax.boxplot(x)`) draws a box plot from the data in `x`; it accepts array-like data and can draw one or more boxes. The box extends from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3) of the data, with a line at the median. The whiskers extend from the box to the farthest data point lying within 1.5x the interquartile range (IQR) from the box; points past the end of the whiskers are flier points (outliers). For example, if Lagos's box runs from Q1 = 20 minutes to Q3 = 30 minutes, the interquartile range (IQR) is the length of the box: 30 - 20 = 10 minutes. The whiskers can then reach at most 1.5 x 10 = 15 minutes beyond the box -- no lower than 5 minutes and no higher than 45 minutes -- so a 50-minute Lagos delivery would be drawn as a separate flier point.

Passing a sequence of 1D arrays as `x` draws one box for each array in the sequence; `tick_labels=[...]` labels each boxplot's tick accordingly instead of leaving it as a numeric value. `lagos_times = orders.loc[orders["city"] == "Lagos", "delivery_time_minutes"]` pulls out just the Lagos delivery times by boolean filtering, and `abuja_times`/`kano_times` are built the same way for the other two cities. `plt.boxplot([lagos_times, abuja_times, kano_times], tick_labels=["Lagos", "Abuja", "Kano"])` then draws three boxes side by side, one per city, each labeled with its city name instead of 1, 2, 3.

context.concept_name: Matching chart type to the analytical question

coverage.learning_objective: Match a chart type (bar, histogram, line, scatter, or box) to the analytical question being explored during one's own analysis.

required_facts.statement: A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories.
plt.hist() bins a numeric variable, counts values per bin, and draws the distribution as bars.
Line graphs are best when you want to show how a value changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other.
A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables plotted along the horizontal and vertical axis.
Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side.

teaching_blocks.content: With five chart types available, the question during your own exploration is which one actually answers the question you're asking of the data.

A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories -- average delivery time per city, for instance. `plt.hist()` bins a numeric variable, counts values per bin, and draws the distribution as bars -- useful for how delivery times themselves are spread out. Line graphs are best when you want to show how a value changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other -- average delivery time across the days of the week. A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables plotted along the horizontal and vertical axis -- whether distance and delivery time move together. Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side -- the full spread of delivery times across several cities at once, not just their averages.

Picking a chart type during exploration comes down to naming what you're actually asking: a category comparison, a single variable's spread, a trend over time, a relationship between two variables, or a spread comparison across several groups.

video_need.reason: Walking through the same delivery dataset rendered as each candidate chart type, side by side, makes the decision process more concrete than the text's recap, though the recap of each chart's purpose already orients a learner.

`seaborn.barplot(data=..., x=..., y=...)` visualizes an aggregate statistical estimate for each category as a bar; its default estimator is the mean, and it draws an error bar (uncertainty indicator) around each bar by default. `sns.set_theme(style=..., palette=...)` changes the global defaults for all plots using the matplotlib rcParams system, so it affects matplotlib plots too, even ones not made with seaborn. Because it works by changing global defaults, calling `sns.set_theme()` changes how plots drawn after that call look -- it does not go back and restyle a figure you already drew and displayed earlier.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you want to show the delivery-time histogram and the distance/delivery-time scatter plot together, side by side, instead of as two separate figures.

`fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols)` creates a Figure containing a grid of Axes with the given number of rows and columns (for example `plt.subplots(2, 2)` creates a 2x2 grid). `fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2)` creates one Figure holding four Axes arranged in two rows and two columns.

Each Axes in the returned grid is indexed separately (for example `axs[0, 0]`) and plotting/labeling calls made on one Axes only affect that panel. `axs[0, 0].hist(orders["delivery_time_minutes"])` draws the delivery-time histogram into the top-left panel, and `axs[0, 1].scatter(orders["distance_km"], orders["delivery_time_minutes"])` draws the distance/delivery-time scatter into the top-right panel without disturbing the first.

clusters.title: Bar Charts and Histograms
clusters.reasoning: Bar charts (categorical comparison) and histograms (continuous distribution) are often confused because they look similar. Showing them together makes the critical distinction immediately visible: bar charts have gaps between bars and compare categories; histograms have no gaps and show distribution. The contrast is the core learning, making them ideal for a cluster.

clusters.title: Line Plots and Scatter Plots
clusters.reasoning: Line plots (trends over an ordered axis, typically time) and scatter plots (relationship between two continuous variables) are both two-variable charts that learners often conflate. Showing them together makes the distinction clear: line plots connect ordered points to show trend; scatter plots show correlation between unordered pairs. Box plots show distribution rather than relationships and are better shown separately.

clusters.title: Seaborn DataFrame Plotting and Statistical Functions
